newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam coffee trade slows, mouldy beans linger.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam coffee trade slows, mouldy beans linger.

text.p: Trading in Vietnam's robusta coffee crop has slowed recently after prices in London and New York fell, while concerns about mouldy beans from the local harvest continue to linger, regional dealers said on Wednesday.

Vietnamese coffee prices have failed to reflect the recent slide in coffee futures, the dealers said. LIFFE's January contract ended on Tuesday at US$1,339 a tonne, down sharply from its November peak of $1,476 a tonne.

"The trade is not willing to pay the differential at this point. In general, the industry is well-covered. There's very little new business going on," a senior trader for a European commodity house said.
"London has dropped a lot so buyers are expecting Vietnam's prices to fall as well," a Singapore-based coffee trader said.
"I can understand that people are waiting for the differential to come off," a coffee dealer for a U.S. trading house added.
Regional traders said they expected the January contract to take another hit when London opened later on Wednesday, but that they believed any losses would be limited.
"Technically, it's still very bad," a trader said, adding that coffee would probably face more fund selling in the afternoon.
"It's due to open $10 lower, although the downside should be limited," another dealer said.

Quality problems continue to plague Vietnam's robusta crop because heavier-than-usual rains have prevented the beans from drying properly. The rains have also made it difficult to transport the beans to the main port of Ho Chi Minh City.
"Some people are accepting a small amount of mouldy beans. But everybody is scrambling around to control the quality as much as possible," one trader said.
"There is some concern that all the rains may make the coffee beans more mouldy," a dealer in Singapore said.
Another trader was more optimistic.
"I don't think it's that bad. It's just taking more time to dry the coffee beans," the dealer said.
Traders said the real test would come when coffee shipped from Vietnam reached roasters in the United States and Europe.
"It would really come down to the tolerance level of the roasters," a trader said.
Vietnam's November coffee exports reached about 20,000 tonnes, down from an estimated 26,000-30,000 tonnes in the same month last year, the traders said.
Vietnam's benchmark Grade 2 coffee was quoted by regional traders at around $1,020-$1,050 a tonne FOB Saigon for prompt shipment, down slightly from last week's $1,070-$1,090 a tonne.

In Indonesia, the development of the coffee plants looks good and dealers expect a bumper crop when the harvest begins in earnest in March 1997. The crop in Indonesia has been hit by drought in the past two seasons.
"Weather conditions have been favourable," one dealer said.
Indonesia's Grade 4 coffee was priced at around $1,800-$1,250 a tonne FOB Panjang, almost unchanged from last week's $1,200-$1,250.
Three tonnes were traded on the January coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange on Tuesday and the contract settled at $1,195 a tonne.
Five tonnes were sold on Monday. Two tonnes of the January contract ended at $1,222 a tonne while three tonnes of the March contract finished at $1,182 a tonne.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
